data.title: Sedliacka Dubová – Žiar, a Hallstatt hillfort under a ruined church
data.excerpt: The hill of Žiar, also called Hrádok, rises above the valley of the Orava and carries the ruins of a small church — and beneath them the rampart of a Hallstatt hillfort. Excavation in 1954 showed a fortified settlement whose neck rampart stood some 6 m high and which burnt down, together with the settlement below it, in the Middle La Tène period.
data.metaTitle: Sedliacka Dubová – Žiar, a Hallstatt hillfort in Orava
data.metaDescription: The hill of Žiar above Sedliacka Dubová hides a fortified Hallstatt settlement, identified in 1954; a church ruin now leans against its 6 m neck rampart.

children.text: The earliest history of the place where the ruins of the small church stand reaches far back into prehistory. The very name of the hill — Žiar, or Hrádok — on which the church was built suggests that a fortified structure once stood here. The archaeological excavation carried out in 1954 made it clear that this was a fortified Hallstatt settlement.

The Hallstatt period, as we call the Early Iron Age, was the prehistoric period from 700 to 400 BC. At that time the occupation of Orava was relatively dense. Fortified settlements are archaeologically attested, for example, at Tvrdošín, Podbiel, Istebné – Hrádok, Vyšný Kubín – Tupá and Ostrá skala, Žaškov – Hrádok, Jasenica – Hrdoš, Medzibrodie, Oravský Podzámok and Sedliacka Dubová – Žiar, and so are urn graves and unprotected settlements. All the fortified settlements have the character of an upland hillfort, that is, they were built on a hill, and they were placed in such positions that one hillfort could be seen from another. A defensive system built in this way, using smoke signals, formed a strong defensive whole belonging to the local principality. The valleys of the Orava and its side tributaries provided agricultural land, but above all convenient crossings, and they made communication with the main trade routes running through Orava and Liptov possible. The importance of these routes is reflected in the hoards of bronzes from Komjatná, Žaškov, Osádka, Pucov, Istebné – Hrádok, Nižná and Krásna Hôrka.

The small fort at Dubová is therefore not an isolated structure. It was situated on the crown of a hill that cuts sharply into the valley of the Orava, through which an old trade route ran. The present-day remains of the fortified precinct of the church at Dubová rest directly against the massive rampart of the Hallstatt hillfort. According to research so far, this was a structure with predominantly fortress-like features.

The dominant feature of the fort was a neck rampart about 6 m high, separating the fort hill from the rest of the ridge (the neck) on the northern side. The core of the rampart was a grillage-and-box construction of round timber filled with red burnt clay. The outer side of the rampart was provided with a supporting stone wall, which increased its defensive capacity. Its rear part sloped gently down into the enclosure. At the highest point of the rampart there was probably a timber watch post – a varta – from where the garrison of the fort had the best view of the approach road and of the whole surrounding country. As a whole, the earthen neck rampart gave the impression of a massive bastion, which was the key element in the defences of the Hallstatt hillfort.

The rest of the fortification was secured by a timber defensive gallery 4 metres wide, built on a stone footing 1 metre high. The gallery was probably faced on the outside with sandstone blocks and covered with a timber roof. The most accessible approaches to the defences were secured by a wedge-shaped ditch 2 metres deep. The entrance to the fort was secured by a gate tower and a bridge across the ditch.

children.text: As I have said, the hillfort served above all a military purpose, so the dwellings were used mainly as quarters for the soldiers and for the captain of the fort. The buildings in the enclosure were put up at least 9 metres from the defensive gallery, and sherds and daub were found at their original positions.

Below the fort hill lay a settlement, where the main economic life of the surrounding population took place. The settlement below the hillfort stood on the site of the present-day village of Sedliacka Dubová, in the street running from the village office to the cemetery, where the foundations of several Hallstatt farmsteads and sherds of Hallstatt character were uncovered; but thickened rims of combed vessels already containing graphite, from the Early La Tène period, have appeared as well. The Hallstatt houses were built in stepped rows on the hillside of Žiar, because at that time the Orava could still flood the valley.

We know very little about the history of the small fort at Dubová; we can only date its demise to the Middle La Tène period, in the 3rd to 2nd century BC. The cause of its demise was a fire that burnt both the fort and the settlement below it. It is assumed that it perished together with the hillfort at Istebné. Both hillforts were probably captured and burnt down.
